evidence.text: Search API 5xx responses increased when index-shard p99 latency rose from 110 ms to 4.8 s during a scheduled segment merge.
API CPU stayed below 48% and memory below 55% throughout the incident, including on hosts returning 5xx responses.
The API client retries a timed-out search twice immediately against the same shard set; retry volume reached 2.6 times normal request volume.
Index-shard CPU climbed from 62% to 98% after retry volume increased, while disk queue depth tripled.
Adding four API replicas reduced per-host API CPU but did not change index latency, 5xx rate, or queue age.
Increasing the API timeout from 2 s to 8 s cut 5xx responses by 31% but increased median end-user latency and grew the request backlog.

A five-minute canary limited each request to one retry with exponential backoff. During the canary index request volume fell 18% and shard p99 improved from 4.8 s to 3.9 s; two canary shards also completed merge phases during the interval, so the improvement cannot be attributed to retry policy alone.

Across affected shards, shards still in active segment merge had 2.1-3.4 times the disk queue depth of same-hardware shards not currently merging. The first affected shard to finish its merge saw p99 latency fall before the others, without a change in API capacity.
Network interface error counters on sampled API and index hosts remained at baseline; packet captures were not retained.
The autoscaler only observes API CPU and request count; it does not observe index latency, merge state, or shard disk queue depth.
Alert suppression in a test environment changed pager volume but had no measurable effect on request rate or index latency.
One unaffected shard was on identical hardware but had not entered segment merge during the incident window.
After the merge completed naturally, retry volume and index latency both returned toward baseline without removing API replicas.
A query-cache configuration change had been deployed to the API tier 35 minutes before the incident; the same change was present in an unaffected region with comparable traffic.
The proportion of long-tail search terms increased by 6% during the incident, but the same query-mix shift appeared on unaffected shards that were not in segment merge.

hypotheses.text: Insufficient API compute capacity was the primary mechanism producing the search failures.
Segment-merge pressure on index shards initiated the latency increase.
Immediate retries amplified index load during the segment merge.
Network packet loss between API and index hosts materially contributed to the incident.

actions.text: Add more API replicas whenever index latency rises.
Limit retries with backoff and add a circuit breaker keyed to index health.
Stagger or throttle segment merges when shard disk pressure crosses a safe threshold.
Raise API timeouts further so fewer requests return 5xx.
Suppress the search-latency alert during merge windows.
